course_notes: Extension modules m10–m17 cover S21–S38 and follow the existing page's colour contrast. Amber is the population / model side: the parameter (μ, σ, p, λ, N) and the assumed distribution. Teal is the sample / data side: the statistic (x̄, s, p̂, r, n) and what we compute or infer. Both instructors return to this repeatedly: 'a statistic estimates a parameter'; 'n−1 makes s² unbiased for the population σ², not an unbiased estimate of s'. Instructors: Prof. Pritee Sharma (economics, School of Sustainability, IIT Indore), S21–S30: data, sampling, descriptive statistics, sampling distributions, sample size. Dr. Ruchi Sharma (HSS, IIT Indore), S31–S38: discrete and continuous distributions, correlation, start of regression. Units and currencies: ₹ lakhs and crores (sales, profits, bank loans, outlets, WTP), USD (weekly salaries, stocks, income brackets), plus hours, days, miles, lb, kg. Two z-table conventions are in use and the page must label which one each widget uses. Pritee's table is a half-table (area from 0 to z; add or subtract 0.5). Ruchi's table is cumulative (Φ(z) = P(Z ≤ z); use Φ(−z) = 1 − Φ(z)). Exam statements from the notes: an end-term exam around 23 November, one paper combining both instructors. It is sent as a PDF; answers are handwritten on white paper, merged into one file and uploaded; camera-proctored (S30, S31). Pritee's 25 marks: 15 end-sem + 5 individual assignment + 5 participation. Her syllabus runs up to and including sample-size estimation; proportions, the sampling distribution of proportions and CLT-for-proportions are excluded ('for understanding only'). Ruchi's 25 marks: 10 handwritten assignment + 15 end-term. The Poisson-as-limit derivation and the Poisson variance proof are not examined. 'Is it binomial?' answers must name the violated condition. Never name students; the midterm example (87 vs 73) should say 'a student scoring 87 / 73'. Existing modules to refer back to rather than repeat: m6 (distribution formulas, MGFs), m7 (normal, CLT theory), m8 (Chebyshev), m9 (covariance, joint distributions).

modules.plan:
Module 'Where data come from and how samples are drawn' (S21–S23). Content type: framework + case. ZERO widgets; use cards plus one decision table.
Cheat cards:
- Population (N) vs sample (n); parameter (μ, σ) vs statistic (x̄, s); a census gives parameters but is costly. Workflow: sample → statistic → estimate parameter.
- Descriptive statistics describe only the sample (the 35-student class exam: no claim about the university); inferential statistics come later.
- Primary data (survey, experiment, in-depth interview, observation, focus group) vs secondary data (Census every 10 yrs, NSSO every 4–5 yrs, IHDS, IMD, Forest Survey of India). Advantages and disadvantages of each. Secondary data lets you build panels (districts × years).
- 'Primary or secondary is relative to the user'. Use metadata to check the collector's purpose.
- Survey modes table: mail / personal / telephone / web, with trade-offs.
- Nested circles: population → sampling frame → sample → response. Errors at each stage: frame, chance, response. Instructor's taxonomy: sampling error = frame + chance + response; total = sampling + non-sampling (measurement). Note that textbooks classify these differently.
- Fix the instrument first: reliable, valid, well constructed.
- Five response-error types: subject lies; subject mistake; interviewer mistake; interviewer cheats; interviewer effects. Instrument error (a misunderstood question) is distinct from response error. Nonresponse error = many people not answering, not wrong answers.
- Probability sampling (known non-zero chance): SRS with a random-number table; systematic with k = N/n; stratified (homogeneous, non-overlapping strata, then SRS within each).
- Non-probability sampling, seven methods: convenience/purposive, judgment, quota (proportional strata, non-random within), cluster/area (take whole groups), multi-stage, sequential (stop at saturation), snowball.
- Hypothesis preview: Ha/H1 = your claim; H0 = its negation; 'the null is rejected'.
Decision table (case) 'which design?': rare trait → non-probability; most units relevant → SRS; known strata needing representation → stratified (random within) vs quota (proportional only); hidden or sensitive behaviour → snowball; whole affected group → cluster; n unknown, stop at saturation → sequential.
Notes and stories (cite sessions), each as a card:
- Election polls of ~1,000: 'Why 1,000? That also we will see' (S21; the payoff is m14).
- LED bulbs 5/500 (S21).
- Senior well-dressed interviewer asking about exam cheating: the interviewer effect (S21).
- Natural experiment: an unemployment-transfer policy in 2016, NSSO consumption ±3 years before/after (S21).
- IHDS latest public round 2012 is outdated for 2026 poverty work, especially after COVID (S21).
- Asking people about temperature is subjective; use IMD instead (S21).
- Myntra reusing its own feedback data is still primary (S21).
- Infrastructure vs forest conservation: secondary data to pick Madhya Pradesh, then a primary survey (S21).
- Smartboard live captions: treatment vs control group (S22).
- Frame error: 'physically disabled' includes visually impaired students who cannot use captions (S22).
- Chance error: every unit drawn from one region (S22).
- Field investigator ticks 'no fridge, no motorbike' because a house 'looks poor' (S22).
- Elderly conservatively dressed woman vs a young interviewer with tattoos asking about drugs (S22).
- Hotel ratings given with staff standing nearby; HR burnout survey; '3 hours of exercise' (S22).
- Walking into a village 'randomly' is not random (S22).
- COVID: hospital records allow SRS; contact tracing is non-probability (S22).
- Diabetes drug: 7–10% prevalence makes probability sampling wasteful (S22).
- Uncontacted Andaman community: exploratory study → hypothesis (S23).
- Travel Cost Method at a tiger reserve gate (S23).
- 'Roadside research': the first village by the highway gets surveyed again and again. Joke: 'Kerala is a convenience sample' (S23).
- Why car showrooms are 'distributors': diminishing marginal utility, so sell the first unit to as many buyers as possible. New features let buyers be 'first' (S23).
- Flood cluster plus unflooded comparison households: assets + livelihood lost vs livelihood only (S23).
- Morbi ceramic cluster (S23).
- Multi-stage on states with >30% area under agriculture. The lecturer calls it non-probability because excluded states' districts get zero chance; textbooks often call it probability (S23).
- WTP for clean water: stop when responses saturate in ₹80–1,000 (S23).
- Snowball for bribe-taking; the Amway analogy (S23).
- Repeated warning: 'bigger n is not better, representativeness is'.
- The lecturer wants original examples and rejects ones that copy an earlier example's structure.
Worked problems:
1. Which sample is better: 2,000 at 90% response or 10 lakh at 20%?
2. Stratified 10% allocation (1000/3500/500) and quota 10% (200/500/100).
3. Systematic interval for 100 of 1,000 schoolchildren; horses 1–380 with skip rule.

Generic inference example: n = 1,000 for ~300 million. Exam class of 35 students. Natural experiment: policy 2016, ~3 years before/after, ~1,000 households. Census every 10 years; NSSO every 4–5 years; IHDS latest public round 2012. Nested circles: population ≈ 5–10 lakh students, frame ≈ 1,000, sample 100. Nonresponse: sample 1 responses 0.90 × 2000 = 1,800; sample 2 responses 0.20 × 1,000,000 = 200,000 (counts derived; lecture gave sizes and rates); verdict: sample 1 is better. Productivity = production / area under cultivation. modules.plan:
Module 'Types of data and levels of measurement' (S24, start of S25). Content type: framework. ZERO widgets; the NOIR table is the centrepiece card.
Cheat cards:
- Qualitative (categorical/nominal) vs quantitative (numerical); discrete (countable: courses taken, runs, footfall) vs continuous (from a measuring process: weight, temperature).
- Variable = an entity whose value varies across cases at one time (HDI for many countries in 2025–26) or for one case over time (India 2000–01 to 2025–26).
- Response options must be exhaustive and unambiguous. Employment: specify the period; >180 days employed vs ≤180 not; add part-time for someone working 4 h/day. Gender and religion options have widened.
- NOIR table: ordered? equal intervals? true zero? ratios meaningful? permissible statistics? Nominal: frequency, mode. Ordinal: + median, not mean. Interval: + mean. Ratio: + ratios.
- Interval vs ratio test: do the zeros of different units coincide? 0°C ≠ 0°F ≠ 0 K, but 0 kg = 0 lb and 0 L = 0 gallons.
- Kelvin is ratio. °C and °F are interval.
- Order of decisions: variable → kind of data → scale; never pick the scale first.
- Principle (S25): collect at the highest level possible.
  - 'Do you smoke?' (nominal) vs 'How many cigarettes in the past 3 days (72 h)?' (ratio).
  - Ranking five soft drinks (ordinal; forces a dislike-all respondent to rank one 1st) vs rating Excellent…Awful (treated as interval; strictly between ordinal and interval).
Notes and stories (cite sessions):
- Jersey numbers are only labels (S24).
- Coding Muslim = 1, Hindu = 2 does not allow an 'average religion' (S24).
- Hurricane Cat 2 is not half of Cat 4; Mohs hardness; ranks 92/82/81 have unequal gaps; military ranks; income brackets where a billionaire and a USD 50,000 earner tick the same box (S24).
- Ranks depend on the choice set: {A,B,C,D,E} vs {C,D,E,X,Y} (S24).
- The humorous ranking slide: dead rat, cow manure, failing this course, chopped liver for a month. Shows how hard it is to rank all-bad options (S24).
- New York 40° vs Buffalo 20° is not 'twice as hot'; body temperature 98°F vs 37°C (S24).
- Petrol pump: fix litres and the bill is continuous; fix rupees and the litres are continuous. Retail footfall vs revenue was left as the lecturer's follow-up task 'go back and think about both examples again' (S24).
- Student-proposed interval examples and the verdicts: 12-hour clock rejected; BMI rejected; rainfall and GDP are ratio. Hardness was first grouped with temperature, then corrected in class to ordinal (S24).
- Lecturer's slip: '300 K is half of 150 K' should read 150 K = ½ × 300 K (S24).
Worked problems:
1. Classify: jersey number, Mohs hardness, °F, K, rainfall, GDP, income bracket, hurricane category.
2. Rewrite 'Do you smoke?' and the soft-drink ranking at a higher level, and say which statistics become available.
3. Fix the employment question with the 180-day threshold and a part-time option.
modules.facts: Religion example: class of 50, 20 Muslim + 30 Hindu = 50; mode = Hindu (30 > 20). Class standing 92, 82, 81 → ranks 1, 2, 3; gaps 10 and 1. Income brackets: < USD 20,000; USD 20,000–49,999; ≥ USD 50,000. Employment: 4.5 months worked; threshold 180 days; part-time 4 h/day. Petrol: 7 L → bill ≈ ₹700.xx; ₹100 → ≈ 0.97 L. Temperatures: NY 40°, Buffalo 20°; body 98°F normal, 100–101°F fever, ≈ 37°C normal. Reference (not stated in lecture): F = 9/5 C + 32, K = C + 273.15, so 0°C = 32°F = 273.15 K. Ratio examples: 100 lb = 2 × 50 lb; 100 kg = 2 × 50 kg; USD 100 = ½ × USD 200. Kelvin correction: 150 K = 0.5 × 300 K. Smoking question window: past 3 days = 72 hours. Soft drinks: Coke, Pepsi, 7 Up, Sprite, Dr. Pepper ranked 1–5; rating categories Excellent / Very good / Good / Fair / Poor / Very poor / Awful (7 categories).

modules.plan:
Module 'Measures of location: mean, median, mode, quantiles, grouped data' (S25–S26). Content type: numerical.
Cheat cards:
- Families of summary measures: location (central and non-central), dispersion, shape, displays (five-number summary, box plot, stem-and-leaf, standardising).
- Mean x̄ = Σx/n; data need not be ordered; it is pulled by outliers.
- Median: order the data; position (n+1)/2; for even n average the two middle values. Three properties:
  (1) robust to extremes on either side;
  (2) a random observation is equally likely to be above or below it;
  (3) Σ|x − median| is minimum.
- Mode: most frequent value; must appear at least twice. Can be unimodal, bimodal, multimodal or none (S25 once misspoke 'multimodal' for all-distinct data; the correct convention is 'no mode').
- Uniqueness table: mean and median are always unique; the mode is not.
- Outlier check: compare mean and median, then plot. Normal data: mean = median = mode.
- Quantiles: k parts need k − 1 cuts (chocolate-bar analogy). Quartiles, quintiles, deciles, percentiles.
- Quartile position rule (S26), with positions n/4, 2n/4, 3n/4:
  - if the position is an integer, average that observation and the next;
  - if not, round up to the next integer position.
  - Positions are not values. Excel may interpolate differently.
- Q1, Q2, Q3 = 25th, 50th, 75th percentiles. Exam percentiles: 40/100 can be the 99th percentile (top 1%).
- Frequency-table mean Σx·f/Σf. Grouped mean uses class midpoints.
- Grouped median L + ((N/2 − cf)/f)·h, where cf = cumulative frequency of the class before the median class. The slide was missing ×h and the professor flagged it.
- Continuity correction: 51–60 → 50.5–60.5 because age is continuous (someone aged 60.4 would fall in the gap).
- Grouped mode L + ((f1 − f0)/(2f1 − f0 − f2))·h.
- Grouped percentile formula: shown on a slide but not read aloud; mark it as the standard textbook form.
- Contrast to carry into m13: the median minimises absolute deviations, the mean minimises squared deviations.
Notes and stories (cite sessions):
- Data 1, 1, 1, 1, 51: four values are 1 yet the mean is 11 (S25).
- Changing 100 to 5000 leaves the median at 5 (S25).
- The in-class absolute-deviation exercise 0, 2, 3, 5, 20, 99, 1000 (S25).
- 'Hand calculations show what happens behind the software' (S25).
- The 99th-percentile score of 40 (S26).
WIDGET 1 'Where is the centre?' (numerical):
- Presets: the lecture's 7-value data with last value 100 / 1000 / 5000.
- Dot plot on a number line with mean (amber) and median (teal) markers.
- A slider c sweeps the line. Two small charts plot Σ|x − c| and Σ(x − c)² against c.
- Readouts: current Σ|x − c|, Σ(x − c)², the median, the mean.
- Verdict line: 'Σ|x − c| is lowest at c = median = 5 (1114 for the 1000 preset); Σ(x − c)² is lowest at c = mean = 161.29'.
- Switching presets shows the median frozen at 5 while the mean jumps 32.71 → 161.29 → 732.71.

modules.plan:
Module 'Dispersion, shape, z-scores and displays' (S26–S29). Content type: numerical, plus framework cards for design principles and charts. Refer back to m8 for Chebyshev and to m5/m9 for variance algebra.
Cheat cards:
- Range: simple, but outlier-driven.
- IQR = Q3 − Q1: robust, but ignores 50% of the data.
- Sample SD s = √(Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1)). Three properties:
  (1) squaring kills the zero-sum Σ(x − x̄) = 0;
  (2) least squares: Σ(x − x̄)² ≤ Σ(x − a)² for every a;
  (3) divide by n − 1 because one degree of freedom is lost to x̄.
- Degrees of freedom illustration: in 2x + 3y = 12, choose y and x is forced.
- Population σ (divide by N, census only) vs sample s (divide by n − 1). Default to treating data as a sample. n − 1 makes s² unbiased for σ² (stressed: 'not an unbiased estimate of s'). S27 said 'overestimate'; dividing by n actually underestimates.
- Variance: additive for independent variables, Var(X + Y) = Var X + Var Y; SD is not additive. Drawback: squared units.
- CV = s/x̄ × 100%. Use it when units or magnitudes differ.
- Units table: mean and SD in original units, variance in squared units, CV in %, z unit-free.
- Skewness via mean vs median. Pearson Sk = (x̄ − mode)/s; not applicable to bimodal data. The 3(x̄ − median)/s alternative is reference only.
- Kurtosis (S29): leptokurtic (tall, narrow), platykurtic (flat, wide), normal = mesokurtic.
- z = (x − x̄)/s. Normal coverage: ±1.96 → 95%, ±3 → 99.7%, ±4 → 99.99%. Chebyshev: at least 75% within ±2 SD (link to m8). Rule of thumb: |z| > 5 is very unusual.
- Five-number summary and box plot; reading skew from whisker and box-half lengths.
- Three principles of experimental design:
  - replication (repeat at least 3 times);
  - randomization (seeds across soil types);
  - local control (adjacent same-soil plots: HYV vs conventional seed).
- Frequency, percentage and cumulative distributions. Class width = range/k.
- Histogram (adjacent bars) vs bar chart (gaps) vs frequency polygon (midpoints joined; better for overlaying several samples, e.g., 10 US states) vs ogive.
- Lorenz idea: 45° line of equality; a bigger gap means more inequality (Gini named for context only).
- Two variables: contingency table and side-by-side bars for categorical data; scatter plot for numerical data, with positive / negative / none / spurious patterns. Lecturer's framing: correlation is descriptive; cause and effect via regression is inferential.
Notes and stories (cite sessions):
- Computer chips: supplier B has the higher mean, but 4 of 10 fail inside the 3-year warranty → 'the mean alone misleads' (S26).
- 15 outlets: range 105 vs IQR 13 (S26). Bank branches: range 8.3 crore driven by metro branches vs IQR 1.2 (S26).
- Sales teams with identical means 52.5: stability vs risk-taking (S27).
- Penny stock vs USD 188 stock: SD says B is more volatile, CV says A (95% vs 6%) (S27).
- Exam data-entry hunt: z ≈ −2.89 traced to a mis-entered score whose true value was 97; z = −3.12 rechecked; after fixes the SD fell (S27).
- 'Assume a sample, use n − 1, unless told it is the population' (S27).
- Box plots side by side to compare many samples (S28).
- Grades vs height scatter shows no pattern (S28).
- Windows 2000 vs 2003 Server side-by-side bars (S28).
- Gender × party contingency table (S28).
WIDGET 'Box-plot reader' (numerical):
- Presets: (a) task-time five numbers 2 / 8 / 10 / 15 / 63; (b) in-class 59 / 64.5 / 66 / 70 / 77.
- Draws a horizontal box plot with the four quarter-widths labelled. Each quarter holds 25% of the data, so a wide quarter means thinly spread data.
- Readouts: range, IQR, left whisker vs right whisker, Q2 − Q1 vs Q3 − Q2.
- Verdict: 'right-skewed: 63 − 15 = 48 ≫ 8 − 2 = 6'; for (b), 'not symmetric, right-skewed: upper whisker 7 > lower 5.5'.
- Five numeric inputs so students can type their own.
- No chart elsewhere in the module; CV and the stock comparison stay as a table card.
Worked problems:
1. The test-score exercise: full summary statistics (mean, median, modes, Q1, Q3, IQR, SD, CV).
2. Sales teams A/B SDs, with the 30.28 vs 31.9 discrepancy shown.
3. Stocks A/B CV.
4. Weekly-salary class width and cumulative counts.

modules.plan:
Module 'Sampling distributions in practice, confidence intervals and sample size' (S29–S30). Content type: numerical. Refer back to m7 for CLT theory; this module replays Pritee's applied problems and her half-table method.
Cheat cards:
- Sampling distribution = the distribution of x̄ over many samples of size n (e.g., heights of 30 grade-5 students per sample).
- CLT (n ≥ 30): x̄ ≈ N(μ, σ²/n) whatever the population shape. E[x̄] = μ (unbiasedness); SE = σ/√n; with large n, s can replace σ.
- THE contrast the instructor stressed:
  - one unit: z = (x − μ)/σ;
  - the mean of n units: z = (x̄ − μ)/(σ/√n).
- Half-table reading: the table gives the area from 0 to z. Add 0.5 for 'less than' when z > 0; subtract from 0.5 for a tail. Φ(z) = 0.5 + half-area.
- 95% CI: x̄ ± 1.96·σ/√n.
- Every statistic has a sampling distribution: x̄ → μ, p̂ → p, median → median, s → σ.
- Estimation formula table (σ known / unknown, large / small n with t, proportion, finite-population correction √((N − n)/(N − 1))). Reconstructed from the standard textbook; the slide was not read aloud. Mark it so.
- Difference of statistics: mean μ1 − μ2; SD √(σ1²/n1 + σ2²/n2); independent samples.

Module 'Which discrete distribution? Bernoulli → Binomial → Poisson, Geometric, Negative Binomial, Hypergeometric' (S31–S34). Content type: numerical + case (classification). Refer back to m6 for MGFs and general formulas; here the focus is Ruchi's derivations, her examples and the classification skill she said the exam will test.
Cheat cards:
- Random variable = a rule mapping outcomes to reals. PMF for discrete, PDF for continuous (her terminology reminder: never say 'density' for discrete).
- Bernoulli: mean p, variance p(1 − p). Derivation: E[X²] = p (briefly misspoken as p²).
- Four binomial conditions: two disjoint outcomes; fixed finite n; independence; constant p. Answers must name the violated condition.
- Binomial PMF C(n,x) pˣ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ˣ.
- Derivation trick for E[X] = np: drop the x = 0 term; x·C(n,x) = n·C(n − 1, x − 1); substitute a = x − 1, b = n − 1; the remaining sum is 1 by the binomial theorem.
- Var = npq via E[X(X − 1)] = n(n − 1)p².
- Mode = largest integer ≤ (n + 1)p, via the ratio (n − k + 1)p / (k(1 − p)).
- 'At most' means ≤; 'at least' means ≥; 'at least one' = 1 − P(0).
- Poisson: counts per unit of time / space; independence and constant rate. Limit of the binomial: n → ∞, p → 0, λ = np. PMF e^(−λ)λˣ/x!. Mean = variance = λ ('a bit limiting'). Scale λ to the window.
- Geometric: trials until the first success. PMF (1 − p)^(x − 1)p; mean 1/p; variance (1 − p)/p²; CDF 1 − (1 − p)^x; support starts at 1.
- Negative binomial: trial of the r-th success, C(n − 1, r − 1)p^r(1 − p)^(n − r); mean r/p; variance r(1 − p)/p². Geometric is r = 1. 'The last trial must be a success.'
- Hypergeometric: the course's only without-replacement model. C(N,i)C(M,n − i)/C(N + M, n); mean np with p = N/(N + M); variance np(1 − p)[1 − (n − 1)/(N + M − 1)].
- Six-distribution summary table and the connections chain.
CASE decision table 'Which distribution?':
- Fixed n, count successes → Binomial.
- Count until the 1st success → Geometric.
- Count until the r-th success → Negative binomial.
- Rare events per unit of time / space → Poisson.
- Drawing without replacement from two types with known counts → Hypergeometric.
- Without replacement with no fixed n → 'neither' (snack example).

Module 'Continuous random variables: uniform and the normal table in practice' (S35, first half of S36). Content type: derivation + numerical. Refer back to m7 for normal theory and the CLT; here the focus is the uniform derivations and Ruchi's cumulative-table procedure.
Cheat cards:
- Continuous random variable: infinitely many values (3.1, 3.11, 3.111…). Probability = area = ∫ f. Valid PDF: f ≥ 0 and total area 1.
- Uniform U(α, β): f = 1/(β − α); the rectangle has area 1. CDF (x − a)/(b − a), with corners at a and b where it is not differentiable; F′ = f elsewhere.
- Uniform mean (α + β)/2 = the midpoint.
- Uniform variance (β − α)²/12, derived via E[X²] = (β² + αβ + α²)/3 using β³ − α³ = (β − α)(β² + αβ + α²). A student's log-substitution was wrong: the denominator is the constant β − α.
- Normal history: de Moivre 1733 as the binomial limit (n large; p, q not small, unlike Poisson's small p). The slide said 'English mathematician'; he was French-born and worked in England. Extended by Laplace via the CLT.
- Normal PDF with 2σ² (twice the variance) in the exponent; the instructor corrected herself. Z = (X − μ)/σ ~ N(0,1). The φ(z) prefactor 1/√(2π) is for the standard normal only.
- Seven properties:
  (1) bell-shaped;
  (2) symmetric, mean = median = mode;
  (3) f decreases away from μ;
  (4) never below the axis;
  (5) linear combinations of independent normals are normal;
  (6) the x-axis is an asymptote;
  (7) X ± Y ~ N(0, 2) and independent for independent standard normals. Flagged as needed for regression.
- μ shifts location; σ² sets spread (the Excel simulation: mean 0 → 2 shifts right; variance 4 → 10 widens).
- Importance list: approximating binomial/Poisson; t and χ² tend to normal; sample statistics tend to normal; small-sample tests assume a normal population; quality-control limits.
- Area property: ±1σ 68.26%, ±2σ 95.44%, ±3σ 99.73%. Critical values ±0.6745 (50%), ±1.96 (95%), ±2.58 (99%), 'critical in hypothesis testing'.
- Three-step procedure: z → table → inference.
- Cumulative table Φ(z): rows give one decimal, columns the second; P(Z > z) = 1 − Φ(z); Φ(−z) = 1 − Φ(z). If a table gives 0-to-z areas (as in m14), add 0.5.
- Probability vs % vs count: ×100 for a percentage, ×1000 for plots out of 1000.
Notes and stories (cite sessions):
- Subway every 30 minutes between midnight and 6 a.m.: wait ≥ 20 minutes (S35).
- U(0, 10) with the student question about the upper limit for P(X > 6): it is 10, not 8 (S35).

Module 'Correlation: Pearson r, Spearman ρ, and where regression comes from' (second half of S36, S37, S38). Content type: derivation + framework. Refer back to m9 for covariance and joint distributions; do not re-teach covariance algebra beyond the shortcut forms.
Cheat cards:
- Bivariate; correlation = co-variation, NOT causation.
- Positive examples: height–weight up to ~18, education–income, income–consumption, supply–price. Negative examples: speed–time, price–quantity demanded (law of demand), vehicle weight–fuel efficiency.
- Time-series components behind co-movement: seasonal, trend, cyclical, random.
- Scatter diagram and its 3 limitations: no number; subjective scale; no significance test.
- Pearson's three assumptions:
  (1) linear relationship;
  (2) many independent causes → each variable roughly normal;
  (3) the forces acting on the two variables are not wholly independent.
- r = Cov/(σX σY), using 1/n forms. Shortcuts: Cov = (1/n)Σxy − x̄ȳ; σ² = (1/n)Σx² − x̄². Combined n-form shown as a textbook equivalent.
- −1 ≤ r ≤ 1 via Cauchy–Schwarz; equality iff the deviation ratios are constant (perfect line). Flagged as THE most important property; a reported |r| > 1 means an error.
- Sign = direction; size = strength. Indicative bands: 0–0.25 / 0.25–0.5 / 0.5–0.75 / > 0.75, and they vary by author.
- Invariance under u = (x − a)/h, v = (y − b)/k, with the proof. The notes add: the sign flips if exactly one of h, k is negative.
- Independent ⇒ r = 0, but not conversely (y = x²). r sees only lines.
- r² = coefficient of determination; r is not a ratio scale.
- Correlation matrix: diagonal 1, simple pairwise only; partial correlation differs.
- Spearman ρ = 1 − 6Σd²/(n(n² − 1)). Derivation: ranks 1..n have mean (n+1)/2 and variance (n² − 1)/12; d = x − y; Σd = 0 as an arithmetic check; Σd²/n = 2σ²(1 − ρ).
- Ties: average the positions, then skip them. Correction Σ m(m² − 1)/12 is added to Σd², summed over tie groups in both series.
- Spearman = Pearson on untied ranks. It is distribution-free; Pearson assumes a normal parent population. Do not rank continuous data (it loses information). Cumbersome for n > 30.
- Partial r12.3: concept, with the standard formula as reference only. Multiple correlation was announced but not covered.
- Regression origin: Galton, 'regression towards mediocrity', confirmed by Pearson. Deterministic (lab sciences) vs statistical (economics, data science) relationships. Error sources: omitted variables, interdependence, intrinsic randomness.
Notes and stories (cite sessions):
- Two car companies over 20 years: sales dip in Pitru Paksha and pick up at Navratri; domain theory should drive hypotheses, 'this is where human judgment enters' (S36).
- Karl Pearson 1857–1936 (transcript '1867–1836') (S36).
- Why do the maths when software computes r: to know the measure's limits so you don't over-claim (S37).
- 'The correlation is 98' → question the method (S37).
- Deflating sales and raw-material series by the same WPI leaves r unchanged; using different, correct deflators can change it, so know why you rescale (S37).
- Nonsense correlations: shoe size vs intelligence; marriage rate vs rainfall; newspaper sales vs crime; intelligence vs physical size (S36–S37).
- Smoking 'establishes' lung cancer: the word 'establishes' makes it false; causality came from other methods (S37).
- Excel: manual r ≈ 0.918, then CORREL; check that both ranges start on the same row (S37).
- A student got Spearman's numbers from plain Excel correlation: that is because ρ is Pearson on ranks (S38).
- Judges A and C think alike; B is an outlier (S38).

- El Niño deficit: crop yield can never be predicted exactly (S38).
